info.bio: U2 (IPA: /ju.tu/) es una banda de rock de Dublín, Irlanda. Formada en 1976, U2, es una de las bandas más populares del mundo desde mediados de la década de 1980. Ha vendido más de 170 millones de discos alrededor del mundo, tiene seis álbumes que han llegado al número 1 en la lista de éxitos en los Estados Unidos y otros nueve en el Reino Unido. U2 es uno de los grupos con mayor éxito de todos los tiempos. Han sido galardonados con 22 premios Grammy, la cifra más alta para un artista de rock.

scenes.name: Nueva psicodelia y big music: Echo & the Bunnymen y U2
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En lugar de descender a lo oscuro, elevarse hacia la luz. Liverpool, que no tuvo punk clásico ni postpunk experimental, quería que la música fuera «una fiesta» (Bill Drummond, Zoo): el club Eric's, las bandas fantasma (The Crucial Three, Big in Japan), Wah! Heat, The Teardrop Explodes de Julian Cope. Echo & the Bunnymen, con el minimalismo aprendido de Television y la voz de Ian McCulloch, graban Crocodiles y Heaven Up Here, respuesta luminosa a Closer, y heredan el público huérfano de Joy Division; Ocean Rain los vuelve estrellas pop. U2, «punk positivo» cristiano y pacifista, guitarra de The Edge como sintetizador, quiere ocupar el lugar de Curtis: War (1983), «Sunday Bloody Sunday» en MTV, The Unforgettable Fire con Eno. Alrededor, la «big music» celta de Simple Minds, The Waterboys, Big Country y la neopsicodelia de The Blue Orchids.

scenes.name: Modernismo británico: de Ultravox a U2
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Los puentes entre punk y pop sofisticado: Ultravox funde punk, el pop robótico de Kraftwerk y Roxy Music (Vienna, uno de los discos que alumbran el synth-pop); XTC perfeccionan el arte de la canción pop como nadie (Drums And Wires, English Settlement, Skylarking); Magazine, Monochrome Set, Squeeze; Japan y su dance-pop decadente; Simple Minds; y U2, el fenómeno más sensacional de las islas desde los Beatles, que unen la vehemencia del punk con el atractivo masivo del pop.

scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: Sonidos que ocupan el espacio y envuelven al oyente; música estática que parece que no está pero que se siente. Eno la concibió como el equivalente acústico a un cuadro o una bella decoración.

podcast.title: Early Formation - Bulletin Board Note (October 1976)
podcast.body: The origins of U2 trace back to October 1976 when 15-year-old Larry Mullen, a drummer, posted a note on a public bulletin board at Mount Temple Comprehensive High School in Dublin, Ireland, seeking musicians to form a rock band. This call attracted several individuals to Larry's kitchen, including Adam Clayton, brothers Dave and Dick Evans, Peter Martin, Ivan McCormick, and Paul Hewson. All seven initially attempted to play through a single amplifier. The lineup eventually solidified to five members: Larry, Adam, Dave, Dick, and Paul, with Paul, despite his initial aspirations, being persuaded to stick to singing due to his poor guitar skills, promising never to touch a guitar again. "It was in the fall of 1976. A 15-year-old kid named Larry Mullin pinned a note to the public bullies and board at Mount Temple Comprehensive High School in Dublin, Ireland."

podcast.title: Stolen Briefcase (Portland, March 22, 1981) – 70 Pages of U2 Lyrics; Returned 23 Years Later
podcast.body: After a show at the Foghorn bar in Portland, Oregon, on March 22, 1981, three groupies visited backstage. After they left, Bono realized one had taken his briefcase containing $300 cash, his visa card in his real name Paul Hewson, tour documents, photos, fan letters, personal correspondence from his wife, and notebooks holding 70 pages of lyrics destined for U2's second album — material that had taken three years to accumulate. The resulting crisis forced Bono to improvise most of the lyrics for the *October* album in the studio, which is widely held to explain that album's unfinished quality. In 2003, a woman from Olympia, Washington, named Danielle Ruyom contacted U2: her friend Cindy Harris had found the briefcase's contents in the attic of a house she'd purchased in Tacoma. After a year of negotiations through multiple layers of U2 management, they met Bono on October 20, 2004, and returned everything except the cash and the briefcase itself. "The only thing that was really missing was the case itself."

podcast.title: IRA Hit List and FBI Assassination Threat – Denver 1987, Arizona 1992
podcast.body: Bono's anti-IRA statement delivered from the stage at a Denver concert on November 8, 1987 — the day an IRA bomb killed 13 people at a Remembrance Day parade — led to rumors he had been placed on an IRA hit list. In 1992 a more concrete assassination threat came through the FBI: because of U2's long advocacy for a Martin Luther King national holiday (opposed by Arizona Governor Evan Mecham), a threat was made that Bono would be shot the next time U2 played Arizona, specifically during "Pride (In the Name of Love)" at Sun Devil Stadium in Tempe on October 24, 1992. The FBI advised U2 not to play the show; when refused, they suggested dropping "Pride" from the set. Bono refused that too. He performed the song with his eyes closed to concentrate on the lyrics; when it ended, he was still alive and opened his eyes to find Adam Clayton standing directly in front of him, prepared to shield him. "Bono sang the whole thing with his eyes closed, trying to concentrate on the lyrics."

The event drew over 20,000 people and stopped traffic, leading Bono to spray-paint "rock and roll stops traffic" on a fountain, for which he was charged with malicious mischief. "U2 is roaring through a North American leg on their Joshua Tree tour when the band thought it might be fun to play a free and unannounced concert in Justin Herman Plaza in San Francisco."

Thanks to the Probation of Offenders Act, no official criminal conviction was recorded, allowing U2's scheduled tour to begin on September 15. podcast.body: On October 2, 1990, U2 boarded a British Airways flight into Tegal Airport in Berlin, which was the final commercial flight to land in East Germany before its official reunification with West Germany at midnight that day. The band traveled to Berlin to begin working on ideas for their next album at Hansa Studios. "On October 2nd, 1990, you two, boarded a British Airways flight into Tegal Airport in Berlin. podcast.title: Zoo TV Tour – Pizza Order in Detroit (March 27, 1992)
podcast.body: During U2's Zoo TV tour in the early 1990s, a notable incident occurred on March 27, 1992, in Detroit. Amidst the show's characteristic use of TVs with cable/satellite hookups, Bono, using a remote control, chanced upon a commercial for a local pizza place. He then used a cell phone to call Speedy Pizza from the stage, attempting to order "10,000 pizzas" for the 21,064-person audience at The Palace. After the third song, three Speedy Pizza employees delivered 100 pepperoni pizzas, which were subsequently thrown into the chanting crowd. Later, t-shirts featuring the phrase "I'd like to order 10,000 pizzas, please" were sold on the tour's next leg. "That whole exchange happened after the third song in the set."

podcast.title: Fan Hearing Loss Lawsuit (1994) – Judge Awarded $34,000 Because No Warning Signs Were Posted
podcast.body: On July 14, 1994, a French fan named Mohammed Falfana attended a U2 Zoo TV show at Stade Vélodrome in Marseille, one of 55,000 people present. Four years later, in September 1997, he filed suit claiming he had lost 75% of his hearing in his left ear and 49% in his right after security guards dragged him into a restricted area next to a speaker tower. U2's position was that he had entered the restricted area on his own initiative and so bore personal responsibility. However, the promoter had failed to post any warning signs advising that standing close to a 100,000-watt speaker system could damage hearing. The judge ruled on this technicality in Falfana's favor and awarded the equivalent of $34,000. "Nice technicality."

podcast.title: Jamaican Airport Shooting (1996)
podcast.body: On January 16, 1996, Bono, his family, friends, and Island Records head Chris Blackwell were aboard Jimmy Buffett's Grumman HU-16 C plane, "Hemisphere Dancer," taxiing at Negril airport in Jamaica. Jamaican police mistakenly identified the plane as a drug runner's aircraft and opened fire, causing a terrifying experience for Bono, who compared it to a real-life James Bond movie and whose primary concern was his family's safety. The incident cut short their Jamaican holiday, prompting them to spend the rest of their time off in Miami, and led to a full apology from the Jamaican government. "Jamaican cops suddenly got it in their head that this was actually a drug runner's plane and they opened fire on it like with guns."

When the secret service attempted to take a shortcut through a dangerous, off-limits camera crane area, U2's head of security, Jerry Mele, was run over by their van, sustaining serious back injuries. podcast.title: Mexican Secret Service Incident – December 3, 1997, Foro Sol Stadium, Mexico City, Security Chief Run Over
podcast.body: After playing a 25-song set at Foro Sol Stadium in Mexico City on December 3, 1997, U2 were approached backstage with an urgent request to leave immediately. Three sons of Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo had arrived unannounced without tickets; venue security had waved them and their secret service detail through in a van. When the president's sons and their bodyguards tried to exit through a restricted backstage camera crane area — dangerous due to counterweights — a camera operator told them to leave, causing a confrontation. U2's road crew intervened, not knowing who the group was. Jerry Mele, U2's head of security, placed himself in front of the van to detain it pending police arrival; the van drove over him, resulting in serious back injuries from which he never fully recovered. The next day, U2 were summoned to the president's palace where the sons produced albums for signing. President Zedillo asked that the incident be kept quiet, stating it could have been much worse. "So what could U2 do?"

podcast.title: Presidential Intervention and Cover-up (1997)
podcast.body: Following the incident where U2's security chief was run over, President Zedillo personally called U2, requesting they not go to the press and instead come to the palace to discuss the matter. At the meeting, the President suggested "forget about what happened," effectively using his authority to prevent the story from becoming public. "So the next day, everybody from the van found themselves in the president's office. The sons were there too. With all the albums, they expected to be signed. Zidio said, look, let's forget about what happened. It's going to been a lot worse. You took on our secret service. Best let it go."

Instead of reaching actual fans, Wiseguy scalped these tickets, leading to them hauling in $2.5 million from the tour. This practice was a major reason for the outcry from fans who were unable to secure coveted spots inside the inner stage ring. podcast.title: Learjet Cargo Hatch Detachment (2014)
podcast.body: On Thursday, November 13, 2014, Bono was on a private Learjet 60 flight from Dublin to Berlin's Schönefeld Airport. As the plane approached the German coast, the rear cargo hatch became detached after a "big thud." Eleven minutes before touchdown, at 12:15 a.m., the door blew off entirely, resulting in two missing suitcases upon landing. A piece of the door was later discovered in the Brendan Berg area. "When the plane landed everybody was stunned to find that two suitcases were missing because the door was gone."

concerts.title: Unforgettable Fire Tour (1984)
concerts.body: U2 embarked on their first tour of Australia and New Zealand as part of their Unforgettable Fire Tour. It was during this tour that they hired local roadie Greg Carroll, who later became a full-time member of their crew. "In 1984, U2 went to Australia and New Zealand for the first time on their unforgettable fire tour."

concerts.title: Live Aid Performance and Fallout (July 13, 1985)
concerts.body: U2 performed at Live Aid at Wembley Stadium in London, introduced by Jack Nicholson at 5:20 PM. They were allotted time for three songs, starting well with "Sunday Bloody Sunday." However, the set went "pear-shaped" when Bono's lengthy on-stage interaction with an audience member during "Bad" consumed too much time, causing them to miss playing their planned third song, "Pride (In the Name of Love)." "The band, like everybody else, had only enough time to play three songs, and things started well enough with a version of Sunday Bloody Sunday."

concerts.title: Amnesty International's Conspiracy of Hope Tour (1986)
The Joshua Tree Tour (Second Leg, 1987-1988)
concerts.body: Dallas Schoo became a part of U2's road crew starting from the second leg of The Joshua Tree tour. "He's from Lexington, Kentucky and has been part of the you two road crew since the second leg of the Joshua Tree tour."

concerts.title: Sydney Football Stadium (November 26, 1993)
concerts.body: U2 was scheduled to play the first of two nights at Sydney Football Stadium on November 26, 1993. This particular show was meant to be a rehearsal for a subsequent recorded and broadcast performance. However, due to Adam Clayton's incapacitation, bass tech Edward Morgan stepped in, making it the only time U2 performed with a man down. "On November 26th, U2 was supposed to play the first of two nights at Sydney Football Stadium."

concerts.title: Zoo TV Tour (1993)
concerts.body: During their Zoo TV tour in Australia in 1993, U2 faced an emergency when bassist Adam Clayton was unable to perform due to a three-day bender. The show, which was intended as a rehearsal for a globally broadcast performance, proceeded with Adam Clayton's bass tech, Edward Morgan, filling in. "They were on tour in Australia in 1993 on the Zoo TV tour."

concerts.title: 4L Saul Stadium, Mexico City (December 3, 1997)
concerts.body: U2 played a 25-song set at this stadium on December 3, 1997, which was followed by a bizarre and dangerous incident involving the sons of Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo and U2's security detail. "You too had just played a 25 song set and were coming off stage when one of the security guards said, you need to get into the car and get out of here now."

concerts.title: PopMart Tour (1997-1998)
concerts.body: Willie Williams designed the stage and lighting for U2's PopMart Tour, continuing his extensive work as the band's tour designer. "Willie has designed all of you two's tours since 1983, the Joshua Tree stage, Zoo TV, Popmart 360, all of them."

concerts.title: 360 Tour (2009-2011)
concerts.body: Willie Williams was responsible for designing U2's 360 Tour, adding it to his long list of innovative stage designs for the band since 1983. "Willie has designed all of you two's tours since 1983, the Joshua Tree stage, Zoo TV, Popmart 360, all of them."

concerts.title: U2:UV Achtung Baby Live at Sphere (2023-2024)
concerts.body: U2 initiated a 40-show residency at The Sphere in Las Vegas, beginning on September 29, 2023, performing their special show titled "U2UV." This residency attracted 663,000 people and generated an incredible box office gross of $245 million US dollars, marking the venue's opening act and setting a new standard for artist residencies with its immersive experience. "It opened for business on September 29, 2023, with the first of 40 shows by U2."

concerts.title: Berlin Concert
concerts.body: During a concert in Berlin, Bono's performance of "Beautiful Day" was largely "on point," although he may have been holding back slightly. He relied on The Edge's background vocals to add "oomph" to the performance. "On this particular night in Berlin, things were pretty much on point, although maybe he was holding back just a little."

San Francisco Impromptu Gig
concerts.body: U2 performed an impromptu gig on the streets of San Francisco, which was cited as one of many other legendary concerts meriting historical consideration. "You too is impromptu gig on the streets of San Francisco"

U2 360 World Tour - Research In Motion/Blackberry Sponsorship
concerts.body: The U2 360 World Tour, described as one of the most expensive tours ever staged, was underwritten by Research In Motion and its Blackberry brand. This was one of several corporate sponsorships U2 engaged in. "It was underwritten by Research and Motion in Blackberry."

concerts.title: Vertigo Tour
concerts.body: A global concert tour by U2 that was significantly impacted by ticket scalping bots. Ken Losson, head of Wise Guy, utilized his bot technology to corner the market on tickets, ultimately making a profit of $2.3 million from the tour by outmaneuvering legitimate fans. "His biggest score was U2's Vertigo Tour, where he managed to rack up a profit of $2.3 million by elbowing aside real humans with his bots."
